clue.text: Go off one Caribbean snack

blocks.note: food that goes off rots
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone warns that a single Caribbean snack has gone bad.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'Go off' as describing the snack, but it is the first piece of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Roti is a flatbread wrap, often filled with curry, sold as street food in Trinidad and elsewhere in the West Indies.

clue.text: One short order available when requested

indicators.note: something short is missing its end, so a letter comes off the tail

blocks.note: the number word with its final letter removed
to order is to demand

explanation.surface: A diner places a quick order for a dish that is ready whenever asked for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One short order' looks like a single brief request; split it as ONE cut short, then a word for order.
explanation.definitionFit: Services offered on demand, such as streaming television, can be had at any moment the customer asks.

clue.text: I’m so obsequious, men say nastily

definitions.note: the clue speaks in the character's own voice rather than naming him with a noun

indicators.note: doing something nastily treats it roughly, so the letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: the six letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A fawning flatterer is mocked as men imitate him spitefully.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a self-description: a person who could say 'I'm so obsequious' about himself is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A yes-man agrees with whatever a superior says, a sycophant who fawns and flatters to stay in favour.

clue.text: To live on farmland can be endured

blocks.note: to be is to exist or live
arable land is ploughed for crops; 'on' places it after the first piece

explanation.surface: Life out on the farm turns out to be tolerable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' here means next to, so the farmland word follows the verb for living.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bearable can be tolerated or put up with, however unpleasant it may feel.

clue.text: A better place

blocks.note: surface reading: an improved location, or heaven, where the dead are said to go
setter's reading: one who bets, so a venue for gamblers

explanation.walkthrough: 'A better place' is a stock phrase for heaven; read 'better' as one who places bets.
explanation.definitionFit: Gamblers go to a gaming house to stake money at tables and machines, so it is the bettor's venue.

clue.text: Modest, keeping son comfortable

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece holds another inside

blocks.note: coy means shy or modest
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A modest parent keeps their son snug and comfortable.
explanation.walkthrough: S is a standard abbreviation for son, as in genealogies.
explanation.definitionFit: A cosy room is warm, snug and relaxing, a synonym for being at ease.

clue.text: Brief advice

blocks.note: first meaning: a barrister, whom a solicitor briefs to argue a case
second meaning: guidance offered to someone

explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' looks like an adjective meaning short; in British legal slang a brief is a barrister, the lawyer who argues in court.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrister acting in court is called counsel, and counsel is also a formal word for guidance.

clue.text: Figure in plane has spell with no end of bad pain

indicators.note: having no end means the final letter is cut away

blocks.note: a hex is a witch's spell
agony is bad pain, here without its last letter

explanation.surface: An aircraft passenger is struck by a spell and suffers terrible pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure in plane' sounds like someone aboard an aircraft; it is a shape in plane geometry.
explanation.definitionFit: A hexagon is a six-sided polygon, a flat shape drawn in two dimensions in geometry.

clue.text: It’s often attached to a post or similar

definitions.text: It’s often attached to a post

blocks.clueFragment: It’s often attached to a post
blocks.note: first meaning: a thumbs-up a reader leaves on a social media post
second meaning: resembling, alike

explanation.surface: Something is nailed to a fence post or something of that sort.
explanation.walkthrough: The post is an online message, not a wooden stake.
explanation.definitionFit: Readers tap a thumbs-up on social media updates, and the same word means resembling or alike.

clue.text: In this state one is making a new life

definitions.text: In this state one is making a new life

blocks.clueFragment: In this state one is making a new life
blocks.note: surface reading: someone emigrating to start afresh in a new country or US state
setter's reading: literally creating a baby, the condition of an expectant mother

explanation.walkthrough: 'Making a new life' is a cliché for relocating; taken literally it is growing a baby, and 'state' is a condition, not a place.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names the condition of being a mother or expecting a child, as in maternity leave or wear.

clue.text: Waterproof sheet colleague and I dropped into lake

indicators.note: dropping something into another thing places it inside

blocks.note: Paul is a fellow setter of this newspaper's cryptic crossword, so a colleague of the setter
taken as written
a tarn is a small mountain lake

explanation.surface: A workmate and I sling a waterproof sheet into a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: The colleague is Paul, another Guardian setter, as Vulcan sets for the same paper. A tarn is a small mountain lake, common in the English Lake District.
explanation.definitionFit: A tarpaulin is a heavy waterproof cover of canvas or plastic used to protect goods outdoors.

clue.text: Obvious feature of Middle America

blocks.note: first meaning: clear, evident
second meaning: flat grassland

explanation.surface: Someone points out an obvious trait of America's heartland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feature' here is a landscape feature: the Great Plains cover the middle of the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: Something evident is clear to see, and a broad flat treeless grassland is a geographic landform.

clue.text: Group of cats, one among several that are deadly

definitions.text: one among several that are deadly

blocks.note: first meaning: the collective noun for lions

blocks.clueFragment: one among several that are deadly
blocks.note: second meaning: one of the seven deadly sins

explanation.surface: A band of dangerous big cats includes one among several killers.
explanation.walkthrough: The cats are lions, and the 'several that are deadly' are the seven deadly sins.
explanation.definitionFit: Lions live in family groups called by this collective noun, and the same word names the chief of the seven sins.

clue.text: Tried to restore computer, and gave it another kick?

blocks.note: first meaning: switched the machine off and on again to fix it
second meaning, whimsical: booted it once more

explanation.surface: A frustrated user tries to fix a computer, then kicks it again.
explanation.walkthrough: To boot is both to start a computer and to kick, so the question mark flags the playful literal reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Restarting a crashed machine is the standard first fix, and 'boot' doubles as a verb for kicking.

clue.text: Insist upon intercourse, but soprano refused

indicators.note: something refused is turned away, so that letter is not let in

blocks.note: intercourse is the sex act
S is the abbreviation for soprano in music

explanation.surface: Someone demands sex but the singer turns him down.
explanation.walkthrough: S is the standard abbreviation for soprano in choral scores.
explanation.definitionFit: To exact payment or obedience is to demand it forcefully, so it is a synonym for requiring.

clue.text: Very angry playwright’s heard

indicators.note: what is heard is taken by ear, so the spoken sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: Oscar Wilde, Irish dramatist of The Importance of Being Earnest

explanation.surface: A furious dramatist's voice is heard.
explanation.walkthrough: The playwright is Oscar Wilde; his surname is said exactly like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who goes wild with rage is furious, an informal sense of the word for uncontrolled.

clue.text: Destroy some trees, a real setback

indicators.note: only some of the letters are used, a run lifted from inside the words
set back means put backwards, so the letters run right to left

blocks.note: a run of letters spanning the words, read as written

explanation.surface: Felling trees is lamented as a real blow to the environment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setback' reads as a noun meaning misfortune; split it as an instruction to read the letters backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To erase is to wipe out completely, so it can mean destroy, especially records or memories.

clue.text: The whole lot in English, with remarkable brevity

indicators.note: something remarkable is out of the ordinary, so these letters are made into an unusual arrangement

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
taken as written; 'with' adds it to the letter before

explanation.surface: Everything is said in English, with astonishing concision.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remarkable' looks like praise for the brevity, but it tells you to rearrange it along with the E.
explanation.definitionFit: Every bit means all of it, entirely, the complete amount with nothing left out.

clue.text: Face relaxed?

blocks.note: relaxed is laid-back, read as LAID written back

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a person's expression looks calm.
explanation.walkthrough: Relaxed means laid-back; take that phrase as an instruction, writing LAID back. The question mark warns of the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A clock's dial is its face, and slang also uses the word for a person's countenance.

clue.text: Legendary swordsman does calm exercises

indicators.note: exercising works something about and puts it through movements, so the letters are moved around

blocks.note: the eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A legendary fencer practises calming exercises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swordsman' suggests a fighter; Damocles never wielded a sword, he sat beneath one hung by a single hair.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend Damocles feasted under a blade suspended by a hair, so the sword is his famous attribute.

clue.text: Open water is hateful: I may get left on the beach

definitions.text: I may get left on the beach

blocks.note: the open seas
a hateful experience is hell

explanation.surface: A seasick sailor complains that open water is hateful and fears being stranded.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition speaks in the first person, as the object itself would.
explanation.definitionFit: Waves wash empty mollusc casings up onto the sand and the tide leaves them stranded there.

clue.text: One applying ointment from tray

blocks.note: first meaning, whimsical: one who puts salve on
second meaning: a flat serving dish, often silver

explanation.surface: A nurse takes some cream from a tray to treat a wound.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is an invented agent noun built from salve, ointment.
explanation.definitionFit: A salver is a formal flat platter, usually metal, on which a servant offers drinks or letters.

clue.text: In Colorado, had encounter with visitor from space

blocks.note: CO is the postal code for Colorado
to have an encounter with is to meet

explanation.surface: Someone in Colorado claims a close encounter with an alien.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Visitor from space' suggests an alien; it is a body that passes close to the Sun and returns.
explanation.definitionFit: A comet is an icy body orbiting the Sun that periodically appears in the night sky before departing.

clue.text: Haul into court to obtain small dwelling

indicators.note: putting one thing into another places it inside

blocks.note: to hale is an old verb meaning to drag or haul
CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: Someone is dragged before a judge to win possession of a small house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Haul into court' sounds legal; hale is an archaic word for haul, still heard in 'haled before the magistrates'.
explanation.definitionFit: A chalet is a small wooden house, typically a Swiss-style cabin or a holiday hut.

clue.text: Only Plan A flies for unquenchable optimist

indicators.note: something that flies is thrown into the air, so its letters land in a new order

blocks.note: the nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A cheerful optimist backs only the first plan and expects it to work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flies' looks like 'succeeds', fitting an optimist's plan; it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Named after the cheerful heroine of Eleanor Porter's novel, the term means someone relentlessly hopeful.

clue.text: Expose the flesh of Prime Minister

blocks.note: first meaning: strip the skin off a fruit
second meaning: a Victorian-era British prime minister who founded the London police

explanation.surface: A scandal threatens to bare the body of a national leader.
explanation.walkthrough: The flesh is that of a fruit; Robert Peel was a Victorian British prime minister who founded the London police.
explanation.definitionFit: Removing the skin of an orange bares its pulp, and Sir Robert Peel led Britain's government twice.

clue.text: John, who composed four notes

blocks.note: four letters that are all names of musical notes

explanation.surface: An American composer wrote a piece using just four notes.
explanation.walkthrough: John Cage was the American avant-garde composer of 4'33", a piece with no notes at all.
explanation.definitionFit: John Cage was a twentieth-century American experimental composer, famous for his silent piece.

clue.text: Keep chewing and not speaking

indicators.note: speaking means saying out loud, so the sound of the words counts, not their spelling

blocks.note: 'and not' is nor, which in a British accent sounds the same as the answer

explanation.surface: Someone keeps eating with their mouth full and says nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British speech nor and the answer are pronounced identically, with the G silent.
explanation.definitionFit: To gnaw is to bite at something persistently, chewing away at it over and over.

clue.text: Torment with base wickedness

blocks.note: a bed is a base or foundation layer, as in a flower bed or seabed
evil is wickedness

explanation.surface: Someone is tormented by vile depravity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' reads as an adjective meaning vile alongside 'wickedness', but it is a noun for a foundation.
explanation.definitionFit: To bedevil is to plague or harass persistently, causing continual trouble and distress.

clue.text: Comprehensive classes, back to school

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so only its final letter is kept

blocks.note: genera are classes in biological classification, plural of genus
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Pupils at a British comprehensive school head back to class.
explanation.walkthrough: A comprehensive is a British state secondary school open to all abilities, which is what the surface pictures.
explanation.definitionFit: Something general covers broadly all parts or cases, so it is a synonym for all-embracing.
